q: Which Summer Olympics, scheduled for Berlin, were cancelled because of World War I?
x: Berlin had been awarded the 1916 Games, but they were never held. The next Games took place in Antwerp in 1920.

q: Which Italian resort hosted the 1956 Winter Olympics?
x: These were the first Winter Games to be televised, with the broadcast reaching several European countries.

q: Which Austrian city hosted the Winter Olympics in both 1964 and 1976?
x: Innsbruck stepped in to host the 1976 Games after Denver withdrew, and so became a two-time host city.

q: Which Ukrainian pole vaulter was the first to clear 6 meters, in 1985?
x: Bubka cleared 6.00 m in Paris in 1985. He went on to break the world record 35 times during his career.

q: Which American sprinter won three gold medals at the 1960 Rome Olympics after overcoming childhood polio?
x: Rudolph won the 100 m, 200 m and 4x100 m relay. Italian crowds nicknamed her 'La Gazzella Nera', the Black Gazelle.

q: Which Belgian cyclist, nicknamed 'The Cannibal', won the Tour de France five times?
x: Merckx won his Tours between 1969 and 1974. In 1969 he took the overall, points and mountains classifications in the same year.

q: On which German circuit did Niki Lauda suffer his near-fatal Formula One crash in 1976?
x: Lauda returned to racing just six weeks later. He went on to win the world title in 1977 and again in 1984.

q: Which English racecourse hosts the Grand National steeplechase?
x: The race has been run over fences at Aintree near Liverpool since 1839. Its fences, such as Becher's Brook, are famous.

q: Who in 1875 became the first person to swim the English Channel without artificial aid?
x: Captain Webb took nearly 22 hours to swim from Dover to Calais. He was said to have used a breaststroke and was greased in porpoise oil.

q: Which Frenchman scored 13 goals at the 1958 World Cup?
x: Fontaine scored his 13 goals in only six matches, and France finished third. Brazil, with 17-year-old Pele, won the title.

q: Which country won the 1992 European Championship in soccer after joining the tournament late as a replacement?
x: Denmark replaced Yugoslavia, which was excluded, just ten days before the tournament and beat Germany 2-0 in the final.

q: In which year was the first Wimbledon Championship played?
x: Only the men's singles was held in 1877, with 22 players. Spencer Gore won the first title.

q: Which team won the first modern World Series in 1903?
x: The Boston Americans, who later became the Red Sox, beat the Pittsburgh Pirates five games to three in a best-of-nine series.

q: Which England captain devised the controversial 'Bodyline' tactics on the 1932-33 tour of Australia?
x: Bodyline involved fast bowlers aiming at the batter's body. It caused such anger that the laws of cricket were later changed.

q: How many consecutive baseball games did Cal Ripken Jr. play between 1982 and 1998?
x: Ripken passed Lou Gehrig's long-standing mark of 2,130 games on September 6, 1995. He was nicknamed 'the Iron Man'.

q: At which Melbourne stadium is the AFL Grand Final traditionally played?
x: The MCG holds more than 90,000 spectators. It also hosted the 1956 Summer Olympics.

q: Which sport is played with a stick called a hurley and a ball called a sliotar?
x: Hurling is an ancient Gaelic game, among the fastest field sports in the world. A sliotar is a leather ball with a raised seam.

q: Which sport was invented in 1895 in Holyoke, Massachusetts, as a gentler alternative to basketball?
x: William G. Morgan originally called it 'mintonette'. A visitor suggested the name volleyball because players 'volley' the ball.

q: What is the highest score that can be checked out with three darts in a single turn?
x: The checkout is two treble 20s followed by a bullseye. A 3-dart finish must end on a double or the bullseye.

q: Which club owns Lord's Cricket Ground and was the long-time guardian of cricket's Laws?
x: The MCC, founded in 1787, wrote the first Laws of Cricket in 1788. Lord's is in north London and is called the 'Home of Cricket'.

q: Which American heavyweight boxer retired undefeated in 1956 with a record of 49 wins and no losses?
x: Marciano knocked out 43 of his opponents. He died in a plane crash in 1969, the day before his 46th birthday.

q: In which country was the 1975 'Thrilla' fight between Muhammad Ali and Joe Frazier held?
x: The bout in Manila was the third and final fight between the pair. Frazier's corner stopped the fight before the 15th round.

q: The Paralympic movement grew from games held in 1948 at a hospital in which country?
x: Dr Ludwig Guttmann organized archery for wartime injured at Stoke Mandeville Hospital. The first official Paralympics took place in Rome in 1960.

q: In which event did Bob Beamon leap 8.90 m at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics?
x: Beamon beat the previous world mark by 55 cm, helped by the thin air of Mexico City. It was so far that officials had to measure it by hand with a tape.

q: The marathon distance of 26 miles 385 yards was set at the Olympics in which city?
x: The 1908 course ran from Windsor Castle to the stadium so that the royal family could watch from the start.

q: Which sport is part of modern pentathlon alongside fencing, swimming, shooting and running?
x: The modern pentathlon was devised by Pierre de Coubertin, inspired by the skills of a 19th-century cavalry officer.

q: How much does a men's Olympic hammer weigh?
x: The hammer is a metal ball on a steel wire. It weighs the same as the men's shot put, 16 pounds.

q: Which Rio stadium hosted the 1950 World Cup match in which Uruguay stunned Brazil?
x: Well over 150,000 spectators watched Uruguay win 2-1. The defeat is remembered in Brazil as the 'Maracanazo'.

q: Which Hungarian forward starred for the 'Magical Magyars' and later for Real Madrid?
x: Puskas scored four goals in the 1960 European Cup final for Real Madrid. He was nicknamed 'the Galloping Major'.

q: Which Portuguese star was top scorer at the 1966 World Cup with nine goals?
x: Eusebio scored four goals in a quarter-final comeback against North Korea. He was nicknamed 'the Black Panther'.

q: Who scored two headed goals for France in the 1998 World Cup final?
x: Zidane's goals both came from corner kicks in the first half. France led 2-0 at the interval and Petit added a third.

q: Which trophy did Brazil keep permanently after winning a third World Cup in 1970?
x: The original trophy was later stolen in Brazil in 1983 and never recovered. FIFA introduced a new trophy for 1974.

q: How wide is a standard soccer goal between the posts?
x: That is 7.32 meters. The crossbar stands 8 feet (2.44 m) above the ground.

q: Which Grand Slam tournament was the first to become an open event, in 1968?
x: Open tennis allowed professionals to compete in the major tournaments alongside amateurs. Ken Rosewall won the first men's open title.

q: Which American teenager known as 'Little Mo' won the first women's calendar-year Grand Slam, in 1953?
x: Connolly's career ended at 19 after a horse-riding accident. Her tennis was admired for its accuracy.

q: Who in 1938 became the first man to win all four Grand Slam tennis titles in a single year?
x: The American's feat was unmatched until Rod Laver repeated it in 1962. Budge's backhand was regarded as one of the best of all time.

q: Which former champion lost to Billie Jean King in the 1973 'Battle of the Sexes' tennis match?
x: King won in straight sets in front of about 30,000 fans at the Houston Astrodome and an estimated 90 million TV viewers.

q: The Davis Cup in tennis is named after which American player who donated the trophy?
x: Davis, a Harvard student, designed the competition in 1900 and later became US Secretary of War.

q: Which amateur golfer won the four major tournaments of his era in 1930 and co-founded Augusta National?
x: Jones retired from competition at just 28, after winning the 'Grand Slam' of that time. He was a lawyer by profession.

q: Which Spanish golfer won the Open Championship in 1979, 1984 and 1988?
x: Ballesteros was known for his creative shot-making from trouble. He also won the Masters twice, in 1980 and 1983.

q: Which South African golfer, nicknamed 'The Black Knight', won nine major championships?
x: Player was famous for wearing black on the course and for his fitness. He was one of the first golfers to travel the globe to play.

q: What is the diameter of a golf hole?
x: That is 108 mm. The size was standardized by the Royal and Ancient Golf Club in 1891, based on a piece of drainage pipe used at Musselburgh.

q: Which Scottish course hosted the first Open Championship in 1860?
x: Willie Park Sr. won the first Open, played over three rounds of a 12-hole course, with eight players competing.

q: Which England batsman was bowled by Shane Warne's famous 'Ball of the Century' in 1993?
x: Warne's first ball in Ashes cricket spun sharply from outside leg stump to hit off stump at Old Trafford.

q: Which West Indian all-rounder hit six sixes in one over in a 1968 first-class match?
x: Sobers hit all six off Glamorgan's Malcolm Nash at Swansea, in the first instance in first-class cricket.

q: Which two countries played the first Test match, in 1877?
x: The match was played in Melbourne, and Australia won by 45 runs. Charles Bannerman scored the first Test century.

q: In which Indian city is the Eden Gardens cricket ground?
x: Eden Gardens opened in 1864 and is one of the largest cricket stadiums in the world. It hosted the 1987 and 1996 World Cup semi-finals.

q: The name 'the Ashes' came from a mock obituary of English cricket in which 1882 publication?
x: The notice said English cricket had died and the body would be cremated and the ashes taken to Australia.

q: At which English school, according to legend, did William Webb Ellis first run with the ball in 1823?
x: The legend is widely considered a myth, but it gave the sport its name and the Rugby World Cup its trophy.

q: What were the first basketball goals, nailed to a gym balcony in 1891, made from?
x: Each time a ball went in, someone had to climb up and retrieve it, until the bottoms were cut out of the baskets.

q: In which NBA season was the three-point line first introduced?
x: The ABA had used the three-point shot earlier, in the 1960s. The NBA adopted it after absorbing several ABA teams.

q: Which NBA star was famous for the 'skyhook' shot?
x: Abdul-Jabbar was originally named Lew Alcindor and won six NBA championships. The skyhook was nearly impossible to block.

q: How many games long was Joe DiMaggio's 1941 hitting streak?
x: DiMaggio hit safely in 56 straight games for the Yankees. Many see it as baseball's most unbreakable feat.

q: In which small New York town is the National Baseball Hall of Fame located?
x: A myth claims Abner Doubleday invented baseball in Cooperstown in 1839. The Hall of Fame opened there in 1939.

q: Which Yankees pitcher threw a perfect game in the 1956 World Series?
x: Larsen retired all 27 batters faced in Game 5 against the Brooklyn Dodgers. Yogi Berra famously jumped into his arms.

q: Which team won the first Super Bowl, in January 1967?
x: The Packers beat the Chiefs 35-10 in the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum. The game was then called the AFL-NFL World Championship.

q: Which NFL team completed a perfect 17-0 season in 1972?
x: The Dolphins went on to win Super Bowl VII. They remain the only NFL team to finish a full season without a loss or tie.

q: The Stanley Cup was donated by Lord Stanley, who held which office in Canada?
x: Lord Stanley of Preston bought the original bowl for about 10 guineas in 1892.

q: Which defenseman scored the famous 'flying' Stanley Cup-winning goal in 1970?
x: Orr's overtime goal for the Boston Bruins against St. Louis was captured in a photo of him airborne after being tripped.

q: Which Norwegian figure skater won Olympic gold in 1928, 1932 and 1936 and became a film star?
x: Henie introduced short skirts and white boots to figure skating. She later starred in Hollywood musicals.

q: Which French skier won all three alpine events at the 1968 Winter Olympics in Grenoble?
x: Killy won the downhill, giant slalom and slalom. The slalom was marred by a dispute after rival Karl Schranz was disqualified.

q: Which Austrian won the dramatic 1976 Olympic downhill, in a run famous for its near-crash?
x: Klammer raced the course on the edge of control and won by just 0.33 seconds before a home crowd.

q: Which US state hosts the Iditarod sled dog race each year?
x: The race of over 1,000 miles commemorates a 1925 serum run to Nome, where dog teams carried medicine to fight a diphtheria outbreak.

q: Which British circuit hosted the first Formula One World Championship race in 1950?
x: King George VI attended the race, which was won by Italian driver Giuseppe Farina in an Alfa Romeo.

q: Which Scottish driver won the Formula One world titles in 1963 and 1965?
x: Clark drove for Lotus and won the Indianapolis 500 in 1965. He died in a Formula Two race in 1968.

q: Which Frenchman nicknamed 'The Professor' won four Formula One world titles?
x: Prost won his titles between 1985 and 1993, and had a famous rivalry with teammate Ayrton Senna.

q: Which British driver won the Monaco Grand Prix, the Indianapolis 500 and the 24 Hours of Le Mans?
x: The trio of races is known as the Triple Crown of Motorsport. Hill won Indy in 1966 and Le Mans in 1972.

q: Which heavyweight boxer was nicknamed 'Smokin' Joe'?
x: Frazier won Olympic gold in 1964 and beat Ali in 1971 in the 'Fight of the Century'. He won on points after 15 rounds.

q: Which British rower won gold at five consecutive Olympics from 1984 to 2000?
x: Redgrave won his fifth gold in Sydney in the coxless four. He had been diagnosed with diabetes in 1997.

q: How many apparatus events are there in men's artistic gymnastics?
x: They are floor, pommel horse, rings, vault, parallel bars and horizontal bar. Women compete on four apparatus.

q: How wide is a gymnastics balance beam?
x: That is only about 4 inches. The beam is 5 meters long and stands 125 cm above the floor.

q: Which Greek runner won the first Olympic marathon in 1896?
x: Louis's win thrilled the home crowd in Athens. He was a water carrier, and his victory was the Games' greatest moment for Greece.

q: In which year BC are the first recorded ancient Olympic Games traditionally dated?
x: The Games were held at Olympia every four years for more than a thousand years, until about AD 393.

q: Which Kenyan runner won the 1500 m at the 1968 Olympics in Mexico City?
x: Keino ran at high altitude and beat favorite Jim Ryun by a huge margin. He later helped inspire generations of Kenyan runners.

q: Which Scottish runner, subject of the film 'Chariots of Fire', won 400 m gold at the 1924 Paris Olympics?
x: Liddell refused to run the 100 m because the heats were on a Sunday. He later became a missionary in China.

q: Which Dutch athlete won four gold medals at the 1948 London Olympics?
x: The mother of two won the 100 m, 200 m, 80 m hurdles and 4x100 m relay, earning the nickname 'the Flying Housewife'.

q: Which city hosted the 1948 'Austerity Games', the first Olympics after World War II?
x: Rationing was still in force, so athletes were housed in military camps and colleges rather than a purpose-built village.

q: Which country won the Olympic field hockey gold at six consecutive Games from 1928 to 1956?
x: India won with a total goal difference of 178 to 7 across the six tournaments. Dhyan Chand was its star.

q: Which Asian nation reached the World Cup semi-finals in 2002 as co-host?
x: The Koreans beat Italy and Spain on the way, before losing to Germany in the semi-finals and finishing fourth.

q: Which African nation became the first to reach a World Cup quarter-final, in 1990?
x: Cameroon, led by veteran Roger Milla, lost to England 3-2 after extra time in the quarter-final. Milla celebrated his goals with a corner-flag dance.

q: Which club won the first five European Cups, from 1956 to 1960?
x: Real Madrid, led by Alfredo Di Stefano and Ferenc Puskas, beat Eintracht Frankfurt 7-3 in the 1960 final at Hampden Park.

q: Which Scottish club became the first British team to win the European Cup, in 1967?
x: Celtic beat Inter Milan 2-1 in Lisbon, with a team all born within about 30 miles of Glasgow. They became known as the 'Lisbon Lions'.

q: What is the oldest national football competition in the world, founded in 1871?
x: The first final in 1872 was won by Wanderers, who beat the Royal Engineers 1-0 at the Kennington Oval.

q: Antonin Panenka chipped a famous penalty to win the Euro 1976 final for which country?
x: The penalty beat West Germany's goalkeeper Sepp Maier in the first-ever European Championship final to be decided by a shootout.

q: Which Italian defensive system, meaning 'door-bolt', became famous in the 1960s?
x: Inter Milan coach Helenio Herrera used it to win two European Cups. It focused on a strong, organized defense and quick counter-attacks.

q: Which ancient Chinese ball game is recognized by FIFA as an early form of football?
x: Cuju, which means 'kick ball', was played during the Han dynasty more than 2,000 years ago, with players aiming a ball into a net.

q: Which English club, founded in 1857, is recognized as the world's oldest football club?
x: Sheffield FC wrote the Sheffield Rules, which influenced the modern game, including the introduction of corner kicks and heading the ball.

q: Which team beat the 'Magical Magyars' of Hungary in the 1954 World Cup final?
x: Hungary had been unbeaten for four years. West Germany came back from 2-0 down to win 3-2 in what is called the 'Miracle of Bern'.

q: In cricket, a googly is a deceptive delivery bowled by which type of bowler?
x: It looks like a normal leg break but turns the other way. It was invented by English bowler Bernard Bosanquet around 1900, so it is also called a 'bosie'.

q: Which bearded Victorian is regarded as cricket's first superstar?
x: Grace played first-class cricket for 44 years and was also a doctor. His beard made him one of the most recognizable Britons of his time.

q: How many hurdles must athletes clear in the 400 m hurdles?
x: The hurdles are spaced 35 meters apart. Each is 91.4 cm high for men and 76.2 cm for women.

q: Which American won four gold medals at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics, matching Jesse Owens's feat?
x: Lewis won the 100 m, 200 m, long jump and 4x100 m relay, the same four events as Owens in 1936.

q: Which Finnish runner won both the 5,000 m and 10,000 m at the 1972 and 1976 Olympics?
x: Viren fell in the 10,000 m in 1972 but still got up to win with a world record. He repeated the double four years later.

q: How many teams took part in the first World Cup in 1930?
x: Only four European teams made the long sea voyage to Uruguay: Belgium, France, Romania and Yugoslavia.

q: The Cresta Run, near St. Moritz, is a famous course for which sport?
x: Riders slide headfirst on a small sled down a natural ice channel. The run was first built in the 1880s by British visitors.

q: In which Canadian city was the first recorded indoor ice hockey game played in 1875?
x: The game took place at the Victoria Skating Rink. It used a wooden puck rather than a ball to prevent it from hitting spectators.

q: Which American became the first Black man to win the Wimbledon singles title, in 1975?
x: Ashe stunned the heavily favored Jimmy Connors in the final. He had also won the US Open in 1968.

q: In which country did 17-year-old Pele win his first World Cup in 1958?
x: Pele scored twice in the final as Brazil beat the hosts Sweden 5-2. He became the youngest scorer in a World Cup final.

q: Which method, named after two statisticians, is used to set targets in rain-affected limited-overs cricket?
x: Tony Lewis and Frank Duckworth devised the system, first used in international cricket in 1997.

q: Which Scottish sprinter won the 100 m at the 1980 Moscow Olympics?
x: Wells won the 100 m by a hair over Cuba's Silvio Leonard. He later said he was inspired by his wife, who coached him.
